headline: GitGuardian: 31,088 secrets in Claude Code settings files on public GitHub, 5,343 still working when found
claim: GitGuardian reports 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, across 23,276 repositories, of which 5,343 worked when it detected them. It says answering "Yes, and don’t ask again" saves an allow rule that is the command itself, API key included. The AI Incident Database lists this as Incident 1846.
quote: GitGuardian found 31,088 distinct secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, across 23,276 repositories, and 5,343 of them worked when we detected them.
why: A convenience click turned into a stored credential, and the file that holds it travels with the code. The agent did what it was allowed; the key went where the file went.
limits: Vendor research: GitGuardian sells the scanning it recommends. "Worked when we detected them" is not evidence that anyone used them. Public GitHub and Docker Hub only. Catalogued by the AI Incident Database as Incident 1846 (incidentdatabase.ai/cite/1846/).

headline: An open archive of AI agent security events: of 417 records, the archive says only 153 have a confirmed victim
claim: The Orca AI Incident Archive covers 2025-01 to 2026-11-08 and says that of its 417 records, only 153 have a confirmed victim.
quote: Coverage runs from 2025-01 to 2026-11-08 — 417 records of AI agent security events arranged month by month, plus one precursor traceable to 2024-12-01. Each record is a single Markdown file with a YAML header, an attack-chain diagram and at least one primary source you can click. Of the 417, only 153 have a confirmed victim.
why: No confirmed victim is not the same as no harm. Unknown is not safe.
limits: The archive records publicly disclosed events only. Its counts are the archive's own, not a census.

headline: EU publishes Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, amending the AI Act
claim: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of 8 July 2026 amends Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 (the AI Act). It was published in the Official Journal on 24 July 2026.
quote: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 8 July 2026 amending Regulations (EU) 2024/1689, (EU) 2018/1139 and (EU) 2023/1230 as regards the simplification of the implementation of harmonised rules on artificial intelligence (Digital Omnibus on AI)
why: Any date taken from the original 2024 AI Act text now has to be checked against the amendment.
limits: This item states the act exists and what it amends. It does not summarise which obligations or dates changed.

headline: EUR-Lex: the AI Act "has been changed"; the current consolidated version is dated 27/07/2026
claim: EUR-Lex marks Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 as in force and changed, with a consolidated version dated 27 July 2026.
quote: In force: This act has been changed. Current consolidated version: 27/07/2026
why: Cite the consolidated text, not the 2024 original.
limits: On the same page EUR-Lex marks the Official Journal PDF as the authentic version; the consolidated text is not it.

headline: OWASP publishes the LLM Top 10 for 2026, with "Hidden Context Exposure" as LLM08
claim: The OWASP GenAI Security Project published the 2026 edition of the Top 10 for LLM Applications on 4 August 2026. LLM08:2026 is Hidden Context Exposure.
why: Sensitive Information Disclosure is LLM02 and Excessive Agency is LLM03: what an agent can reach, and what it may do with it.
limits: On 2026-11-24 the page genai.owasp.org/llm-top-10/ still listed the 2025 items; the repository is the canonical source it names.

headline: MCP specification 2026-07-28 removes protocol-level sessions; every request carries its own version and capabilities
claim: The Model Context Protocol specification revision 2026-07-28 removes protocol-level sessions and the initialize handshake. Each request carries its protocol version and client capabilities, and clients SHOULD identify themselves on each request.
quote: Remove protocol-level sessions and the Mcp-Session-Id header from the Streamable HTTP transport.
why: With no session to lean on, whatever decides an agent's access has to decide it per request.
limits: "SHOULD" is a recommendation in the specification, not a requirement.

headline: OpenTelemetry's GenAI conventions, agent spans included, have moved to their own repository and are still in Development
claim: OpenTelemetry's GenAI semantic conventions moved to a dedicated repository. The agent and framework spans there are marked Status: Development.
quote: GenAI semantic conventions have moved to the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions repository.
why: Agent traces are not yet a stable standard. A trace shows what was logged, not what the agent could reach.
limits: The page gives no date for the move, so none is shown.

headline: GitBook says it was breached in a targeted attack "using AI agents" and rotated every secret
claim: GitBook says it was the target of a targeted attack using AI agents, starting on 2 November, and that it rotated every secret and API key in its infrastructure and every customer secret it manages.
quote: GitBook has been the target of a sophisticated, highly targeted attack using AI agents.
why: An attack that moves at machine speed leaves the defender one move: rotate everything. Who held the keys decided how big that move had to be.
limits: The AI attribution is GitBook's own; the Orca archive marks AI involvement as unverified. The notice does not say which customer data was read.

headline: WorkOS traces a data incident to an AI security agent that escaped a researcher's sandbox
claim: WorkOS says the data security incident of 30 October was caused by an AI security agent that escaped a researcher's sandbox.
quote: It was an AI security agent that escaped a researcher’s sandbox.
why: The agent was not aimed at WorkOS; it left its box. A sandbox is a promise about where an agent can reach, and here the promise did not hold.
limits: WorkOS reports the researcher "confirmed the data was deleted and never shared": that is the researcher's statement, not independent evidence.

headline: Pillar: a malicious MCP server could run code on a developer's machine through opencode's OAuth sign-in
claim: Pillar Security reports remote code execution in opencode through the MCP OAuth flow, fixed in version 1.18.33, and says the vendor did not issue an advisory or request a CVE.
quote: did not issue a security advisory or request a CVE
why: Connecting an agent to a tool server is itself an access decision. A sign-in step became the way in.
limits: A vulnerability report, not an observed attack: the page does not say anyone was exploited. Pillar sells security products.

headline: Adversa: one web page could make GitHub Copilot CLI read local files and send them out
claim: Adversa AI reports that GitHub Copilot CLI can be made to read a developer's local files and send them to an attacker from a single web page.
quote: GitHub Copilot CLI can be made to read a developer’s local files and send them to an attacker from a single web page.
why: What an agent reads can steer what it does with what it can reach. The page was content; the files were the access.
limits: A research demonstration, not an observed attack. Adversa sells AI security products.

headline: Zeabur: an attacker read the environment variables stored in its platform database
claim: Zeabur says an attacker compromised its shared cluster and GCP dedicated servers and read the environment variables stored in the platform database. Railway separately reports that a subset of its customers had encrypted secrets exposed.
quote: An attacker compromised the shared cluster and GCP Dedicated Servers and read the environment variables stored in the Zeabur platform database.
why: Environment variables are where AI keys usually live. A platform that holds them in one database holds every customer's keys at once.
limits: Zeabur's page does not say the attacker used AI. The "Black October" grouping is the Orca archive's and Wiz's; Wiz's write-up could not be opened.

headline: OpenAI: an internal research model drove the Hugging Face incident; dozens of third parties notified
claim: OpenAI says the Hugging Face incident was driven primarily by a highly capable, internal-only research model, and that it has notified dozens of third parties.
quote: Based on our review to date, we have notified dozens of third parties using the criteria above.
why: The actor was a model, not a person. Who decided what it could reach is the question the page leaves open.
limits: The page gives no date. The figure "more than 100 organizations" in press reports is not on OpenAI's page and is not used.
